Co-Reward is simple and intuitive: it constructs paraphrased views, obtains majority-vote pseudo-labels, and cross-supervises the paired views within GRPO.

The empirical scope is substantial, covering six Qwen/Llama models and seven math, code, instruction-following, and general benchmarks. Co-Reward improves over majority voting in most Table 1 comparisons and sometimes matches or exceeds ground-truth reward.

Training curves, difficulty-stratified analyses, test-time-training experiments, rephrasing examples, qualitative collapse cases, and an appendix of hyperparameters provide useful diagnostics beyond endpoint accuracy.
weaknesses: The central comparison is confounded by data and compute. Co-Reward generates rollouts for both original and rewritten questions, whereas the reported baselines appear to process only one view. Table 3 compares training on either view separately but omits the essential compute-matched baseline that trains on both views without cross-referencing, as well as an augmented ground-truth baseline. Consequently, the gains cannot be attributed specifically to the proposed cross-supervision mechanism.

Final-answer agreement does not establish valid reasoning. A shared systematic error—or even a constant answer emitted for both views—satisfies the proposed reward, so the same trivial collapse remains an optimum. Because both views use the same policy and near-equivalent prompts, their errors are likely correlated; no theoretical argument, error-correlation analysis, corrupted-view control, or adversarial test supports the claimed validity mechanism.

The evidence lacks statistical rigor. Results appear to come from single runs without seeds, confidence intervals, or training variance, despite many improvements being around one percentage point and evaluation using temperature 0.8. Checkpoint selection and whether baselines receive comparable early-stopping opportunities are also unspecified.

The critical semantic-equivalence assumption for Qwen3-32B rewrites is supported only by a few examples. There is no systematic human or programmatic audit, robustness study under faulty rewrites, or comparison across paraphrasers. The method is also limited to tasks admitting reliable answer extraction and equality checking, which weakens its stated generality.

The ablations do not isolate the contribution: there is no same-compute two-view self-labeling baseline, no cross-versus-within-view factorial experiment, and no control using unrelated or answer-preserving surface variants. Moreover, the plotted aggregate “CoReward” voting accuracy counts a case as correct when either of two votes is correct, making it inherently advantaged over the single-view majority-voting metric.

Reproducibility is insufficient: the claimed public code URL is blank, and exact per-model step counts, seeds, checkpoint rules, answer parsers, tie/zero-variance handling, baseline implementations, and test-time-training protocol are missing. The mathematical presentation also contains errors, including a GRPO clipping term missing multiplication by the advantage and a gradient-descent update for an objective defined as maximized.

Several claims and reported numbers are inconsistent. Table 1 and Table 5 disagree on multiple IFEval values, while the claim that general capabilities are preserved is contradicted by drops such as Llama IFEval from 57.32 before RL to about 49 and Qwen2.5-7B MMLU-Pro from 44.76 to 40.51. Co-Reward also does not consistently outperform either majority voting or ground-truth reward.

The conceptual novelty is modest relative to classical multi-view co-training, consistency regularization, and recent consistency-based self-reward methods; the paper does not clearly establish why paraphrase-based cross-pseudo-labeling constitutes a sufficiently distinct technical advance.
